> **What this case shows** — the [ANOVA sibling](../gait-grf-anova-pathology-gaitrec/index.qmd) found the
> vertical-GRF *dynamic range* flattens in impaired gait, but clustered the four pathology classes together.
> A different landmark — the **push-off peak** (late-stance propulsion) — pulls them apart. Because the
> push-off peak is right-skewed, the distribution-free **Kruskal-Wallis** test is the appropriate omnibus.
> Each subject's push-off peak comes from the **certified** `grfLandmarks`; the **newly-authored**
> `kruskalTest` compares the five classes, reproducing base R **`kruskal.test`** **bit-for-bit** and
> **`scipy.stats.kruskal`** to machine precision. The push-off differs across classes (**H(4)=274, p~3e-58**):
> **healthy highest** (1.102 BW), **calcaneus lowest** (1.008 BW).

::: {.callout-tip title="The recipe you'll learn"}
**Workflow** — `grfLandmarks()` per subject → push-off peak → `kruskalTest()` across classes.
**Way of thinking** — when one feature can't separate groups, try another; and when a feature is skewed,
rank it rather than assume normality. The push-off peak, tested distribution-free, reveals a propulsion
hierarchy the dynamic range hid.
**Ecosystem usage** — `PhysioMoCap::grfLandmarks()`, `PhysioAnalysis::kruskalTest()`.
:::

## Proposition

The vertical-GRF push-off peak differs across the five GaitRec gait classes (Kruskal-Wallis H=274.5 on 4 df,
p~3.5e-58); by mean rank healthy controls are highest (1408; 1.102 BW) and calcaneus pathology lowest (632;
1.008 BW); `kruskalTest` reproduces base R `kruskal.test` bit-for-bit and `scipy.stats.kruskal` to machine
precision.

## Question & goal

**The question is discrimination and the right test for skewed data: does a different GRF landmark separate
the pathology classes the dynamic range lumped together, and does a distribution-free omnibus reproduce the
reference?** The ANOVA sibling's open question noted that per-class structure needed other GRF features; the
push-off peak is the propulsion read-out.

## Challenge & approach

For each subject we take the push-off peak (the 3rd landmark of `grfLandmarks`, certified in the
[gait-grf-gaitrec](../gait-grf-gaitrec/index.qmd) case) from the body-weight- and time-normalised vertical
GRF, and compare the five classes with `kruskalTest` — chosen over ANOVA because the push-off peak is
right-skewed (skew ~ +0.35) — checking the omnibus H and p against `scipy.stats.kruskal` and base R.

```
GaitRec vGRF push-off peak: HC (208), A (483), K (499), H (364), C (290) → grfLandmarks[3]
  mean (BW):  C 1.008  <  A 1.034  <  K 1.045  <  H 1.050  <  HC 1.102
  mean rank:  C 632    <  A 839    <  K 931    <  H 976    <  HC 1408
  kruskalTest → H(4) = 274.5, p ~ 3.5e-58
     vs base R kruskal.test   → |diff| = 0 (bit-for-bit)
     vs scipy.stats.kruskal   → |diff| ~ 9e-13 (machine precision)
```

## Data

**GaitRec (Horsak et al. 2020)**: processed vertical GRF push-off peak, five gait classes — healthy control
(n=208) and ankle (n=483), knee (n=499), hip (n=364), calcaneus (n=290) pathology — shod, standardised
speed, baseline sessions (one per-subject mean curve). Same matched cohort as the ANOVA sibling. Details in
[`artifacts/data_sources.json`](artifacts/data_sources.json).

## Results

![Left: push-off peak by class (ordered) — calcaneus lowest (1.008 BW), then ankle, knee, hip, healthy highest (1.102 BW). Right: the Kruskal-Wallis mean ranks — healthy controls tower over the pathology classes, and the pathology classes themselves separate (calcaneus clearly lowest), unlike the dynamic range that clustered them. H(4)=274, p~3e-58.](artifacts/figure.png)

*How to read this:* left — push-off (propulsion) is graded: every pathology class sits below healthy, and
the calcaneus (heel/ankle) group is lowest — a plantarflexor-driven propulsion deficit. Right — the ranks
make the separation explicit; this landmark discriminates the pathology classes in a way the dynamic range
did not.

| Class | push-off peak (BW) | mean rank |
|---|--:|--:|
| Calcaneus | 1.008 | 632 |
| Ankle | 1.034 | 839 |
| Knee | 1.045 | 931 |
| Hip | 1.050 | 976 |
| Healthy | 1.102 | 1408 |
| **Kruskal-Wallis H** (df 4) | **274.5** | |
| −log₁₀ p | 57.5 (p ~ 3.5e-58) | |
| vs base R `kruskal.test` (\|diff\|) | **0** (bit-for-bit) | |
| vs `scipy.stats.kruskal` (\|diff\|) | **< 1e-9** (~9e-13) | |

The omnibus equals base R exactly and scipy to machine precision. Values trace to
[`artifacts/pushoff_kruskal_summary.csv`](artifacts/pushoff_kruskal_summary.csv).

## Conclusion

`kruskalTest`, the distribution-free counterpart of the certified `oneWayAnova`, reproduces the reference on
the certified `grfLandmarks`. The transferable takeaway: **the GRF has several landmarks, and they carry
different information — the dynamic range flags impairment but lumps the pathologies, while the push-off peak
ranks them, with calcaneus propulsion the most impaired. Choosing the landmark that separates your groups,
and a rank-based test when the data is skewed, turns one force curve into a graded pathology read-out.**

## Open questions

- The omnibus certifies the five classes differ in push-off, with a healthy-highest, calcaneus-lowest order;
  post-hoc pairwise tests (Dunn) would establish which specific pairs differ, and a multivariate
  GRF-landmark profile (loading peak + trough + push-off) would give a fuller pathology fingerprint. The
  single push-off peak is the most interpretable propulsion read-out. *Documented, not escalated.*

## Using this in your own analysis

| Step | Function | Package |
|---|---|---|
| GRF landmarks (peaks, trough) | `grfLandmarks()` | PhysioMoCap |
| Kruskal-Wallis (non-parametric omnibus) | `kruskalTest()` | PhysioAnalysis |
| One-way ANOVA / Friedman (parametric / repeated-measures) | `oneWayAnova()`, `friedmanTest()` | PhysioAnalysis |

**Reading the result.**

- **push-off peak** — the late-stance propulsive force in BW; lower = weaker push-off, a plantarflexor /
  propulsion deficit.
- **why Kruskal-Wallis** — the push-off peak is right-skewed, so a rank-based omnibus is more appropriate
  than a normal-theory ANOVA; report the mean ranks (or medians) with H and p.

**The recipe, copy-runnable:**

```r
library(PhysioMoCap); library(PhysioAnalysis)

push <- function(M) apply(M, 1, function(v) grfLandmarks(v)[3])  # 3rd landmark = push-off peak
kruskalTest(lapply(class_vGRF_list, push))   # omnibus H, p, df -- bit-for-bit vs base R, machine-precision vs scipy
```

**Auditing the numbers.** Every value on this page traces to
[`artifacts/pushoff_kruskal_summary.csv`](artifacts/pushoff_kruskal_summary.csv), and [`audit.py`](audit.py)
re-checks the omnibus H, p and df, the bit-exact match against base R and the machine-precision match against
scipy, the per-class mean ranks and the healthy-highest / calcaneus-lowest ordering, the design sizes, and
the honestly noted scope (authors the new kruskalTest op; push-off peak from the certified grfLandmarks;
distribution-free because the data is skewed; cross-sectional association).
